l1.summary: Lee tells his brother that La Luzerne is to replace Gérard as French minister, that the 'friend' (adjective doubtful) and his assistants are promoting Deane's [charges?], that French 'faith & friendship' (the first word is written Frenchified) count for nothing beside interest, and that the French nation begins to talk against the alliance. Lee's private opinions, not established facts.
l1.en:
The Chevalier de la Luzerne is named to the place of Gerard, who will a[...]ot leave till the arrival of this
successor. He is a respectable person, brother to the [Bishop?], who is a duke. He was before minister at
Bavaria. I am afraid the [former?] will have done all the mischief, & I foresee much, before his departure. The
[vendible? venerable?] friend, is doing all he can here with his assistants to promote Deane's [charges?]. They are
joined in the same cause & equally wicked. Tho' perhaps I do the latter injustice, in saying so. Certain it is that
such a set capable of every[thi]ng that is villanous, was hardly ever seen before.

I wou'd hint to you, that Frenchified [French?] faith, & friendship, are the same & nothing material to be hazarded
on either. Interest, is the sole guide & the sacrificing every profession & every engagement to this is the
unvariable rule.

l2.summary: Lee reports that Gérard is suspected in Paris of dealings with Deane in merchandise and contracts, and gives his opinion that 'the Doctor', the French consul, Gérard, Deane, Chaumont and Beaumarchais are 'all interested together'; the French court is short of money for the war. Lee's charges, written privately.
l2.en:
I have it from very good authority that Gerard, is suspected here of hav[in]g been concernd with Deane & others, in
merchandise, Contracts &c & that he imposed upon the minister here so as to obtain the Letter for [...]n of wh he
boasts so much. Send me what facts appear on yr side to support this. My opinion is that the Doctor, the French
consul, with you, Gerard, Deane, Chaumont [&] Beaumarchais are all interested, together. There is apparently great
roguery in the business, which time, observation & enquiry will discover. This court, is in a much distress about
supportg the war & mean to call on you for vigorous [exertions?]. But I am afraid they cannot furnish you. Money.

l3.summary: Since Gérard's recall, Lee writes, people in Paris talk of his 'connexion in jobs' with Deane and Beaumarchais; 'a certain person here' is an instrument of those the French court set over him; Congress should resolve that the attacks on the Lees were unjust.
l3.en:
The part of my answer to the Observations which relates to the old Doctor, is so contrived that it may be presented
or not as you judge proper. The propriety of presenting or making public the whole or any part of what I have
written, I leave entirely to your judgment.

Since Gerard was recalled the conversation runs freely about his connexion in jobs with Deane, Beaumarchais & others,
& his [chaplain? character?], is exceedingly reprobated. Mr Ford will give you particulars of things in-

I can only say of certain persons, what many others have said, that if it remains long in their power, it is much to
be feared that they will proceed from jobbing the state secrets, to job the state.

l4.summary: Spain has fifty ships of the line but has not declared; 'the Marquis your Brigadeer' is to return with 2,000 French men (the next word is doubtful), and Lee suspects the French 'wish for a footing'. 'Never will our affairs go well, while Benjamin is here'; whether to present his piece against 'the old Doctor' depends on 'the part taken by John Adams'. Whom 'he is the servant of this court' means is not in the code.
l4.en:
The Spanish court, continues still so lockt up, that no judgment can be formed when they will declare. They have fifty
ships of the line, ready; Their finances are in excellent order, & nothing seems wanting but resolution.

The Marquis your Brigadeer is to return, with 2000 French [troops?]. I do not like the plan. Our alliance has given me
a nearer view of the manner in which things are conducted here, & of their disposition, & I am convinced it is not
safe to let them come too near us, or introduce their [troops?] into our country, or continent on which I am by no
means satisfyd they do not wish for a footing. We must not rely too much on their being restrained by the treaty.
European politicians are much at ease on that head.

Never will our affairs go well, while Benjamin is here.

l5.summary: Lee protests at an anonymous letter of abuse received by Congress against two commissioners, calls Gérard's conduct a 'wicked manoeuvre', warns of a man (name unread) who wants to be 'alternately governor & delegate' in Virginia, and gives plans for two of his brother's sons.
l5.en:
I have received since my last pretty full accounts from Mr Lovell of the proceedings at Philadelphia. I cannot
conceive how it coud have been agreed to receive an anonymous Letter of abuse against two of their commissioners.
Anonymous abuse may be from a notorious Enemy, an interested or an unworthy person, & therefore deserving of contempt
instead of credit. — not seeing any probability of doing good here, I, will probably return to you in the spring. I do
not know whether without any all instructions was calculated to prevent [...] from[...] but certainly it must have
that effect.

Mr S. Adams has informd me that Mr J. Adams wrote him very warmly in my favor, & he convinced me before his
departure that he had done so here. I have sent you Copies of his Letters by a former opportunity which will be the
more important after the wicked manoeuvre of M. Gerard.

l6.summary: On the eve of sailing home, Lee asks his brother whether he could be appointed to Congress from Virginia.
l6.en:
My love to yr family; to London & all our friends. Do you think it practicable to get myself, appoint[ed] from yr
state, to Congress. It will be of great importance. Think of it, in time. Adieu

On the eve of sailing home, Lee asks his brother whether he could get himself appointed to Congress from Virginia.
